summary:
Aragón stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, applies uniformly across the country's autonomous communities, and no Aragón-specific deviation from that position has been identified. A visitor to Aragón is therefore governed by the national rules on recognition, discrimination and sentencing.

Under Article 43, any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry. The right rests on the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution, and it replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. No surgical reassignment is required beforehand, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Spain rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

The same statute defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, and covers discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Anti-discrimination obligations extend to the collection of data broken down by the protected causes.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime in Spain: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately. Both cases fall outside Aragón but show how the national aggravating circumstance is being applied.
tangentialFactors:
Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay, all of which operate a comparable route to legal gender recognition.

A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change. That ranking is a dated baseline predating Ley 4/2023 and should not be read as a measurement of the current regime.

The contrast with the United Kingdom concerns facility access specifically: Spain keys sex-separated spaces to the civil-registry gender marker, whereas the United Kingdom is moving towards biological-sex lines with restrictions decided case by case rather than imposed as a blanket ban.
localsOnly:
Residents of Aragón are subject to the same national provisions as visitors, with additional obligations that fall mainly on institutions and employers: discrimination data collection broken down by the covered causes, and measures adapted to rural circumstances, which carry particular weight in a largely non-urban region such as Aragón.

Ley 4/2023 also bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted reproduction rules, provides parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and strengthens sexuality education. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005.

Minors aged 12 to 16 fall under the law's consent provisions for medical procedures, and gender recognition from age 12 is available under conditions, a provision that proved contentious when the national bill was debated in the Congress.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Aragón-specific implementing decree, regional health-service protocol or regional facility regulation has been sourced for this record; the regional position is reported as resting on the national framework, and any deviated practice by the Diputación General de Aragón or the regional health service remains unresolved.

The two documented enforcement outcomes, in Vigo and Valencia, are first-instance decisions from other autonomous communities. Their reception in Aragón's courts is not sourced, and no trans-specific hate-crime or hate-speech sentencing from an Aragón court has been identified.

Whether the transfobia aggravating circumstance has produced custodial rather than financial sentences in other cases is not established here; the only quantified outcome on record is the EUR 300 fine from July 2026.

The facility rule is reported at national statutory level. Whether Aragón's public premises apply it uniformly, and how visitors are checked in practice, is not sourced.
